title: Tokenize a value, and keep the bulk door shut
summary: An IBAN or a card number your systems must keep somewhere becomes an opaque token; the value itself lives sealed in the vault. The interesting part is not the swap - it is what the vault refuses: bulk redemption without a deliberate, single-use unlock.

steps.label: A person to attach the value to
steps.note: A token can be bound to a person. That binding is what makes it die when they exercise Article 17 - an unbound token would outlive them.

steps.label: Swap the IBAN for a token
steps.note: The value goes in sealed under the PII KEK and scope-bound. What comes back is opaque: it carries no part of the input, so a stolen token tells the thief nothing and works in no other tenant.

steps.label: The same value returns the same token
steps.note: Dedup is a keyed HMAC of the value, never the value. Without it every write would breed a new alias for the same IBAN, and there would be no way to answer 'is this the account we already know'.

assert.message: the same value must dedup to the same token, not breed an alias

steps.label: A card token keeps the shape, loses the BIN
steps.note: Legacy validators check length and the Luhn digit, so the token satisfies both - but the issuer prefix is random. A preserved BIN would leak the bank and the country, which is most of what the number was worth.

steps.label: Redeem one token, deliberately
steps.note: Single redemption is a read like any other: audited, scope-checked, one value at a time.

steps.label: Bulk redemption without an unlock token: refused
steps.note: This is the point of the walkthrough. Bulk is where quiet exfiltration lives, so it ALWAYS needs a second, deliberate act - regardless of configuration. A credential alone is not enough.

steps.label: Mint the unlock token
steps.note: 60 seconds, single use, bound to this client and this purpose, and its minting is on the audit chain. An operator has to decide to do this.

steps.label: A card value that fails Luhn is refused
steps.note: The vault will not pretend a non-card is a card: tokenizing it would produce a token that legacy validators accept for data that was never a card number.

steps.label: Delete a token: the mapping is destroyed
steps.note: The row is the only copy of the sealed value, so deletion is unrecoverable - which is why the action is not in any broad role preset and why the audit record says what was destroyed and who minted it.

steps.label: The deleted token is gone
steps.note: Absent, foreign-scope and expired all answer the same way. A distinguishable 'this token existed' would be an oracle.
